title: Sanctification
summary: These passages connect holiness with belonging to God and with conduct shaped by that relationship. Leviticus calls Israel to consecrate itself because the Lord is holy. In John 17, Jesus asks the Father to sanctify his disciples in the truth. Romans 6 tells believers to regard themselves as alive to God and not let sin rule their bodies; 1 Thessalonians applies holiness to sexual conduct; Hebrews urges the pursuit of holiness. The texts join divine action and concrete practice without presenting identical formulations.
historical_context: The references move from Israel’s instruction in Leviticus to Jesus’ prayer in John and practical counsel in letters to Christian communities. The object’s sources are Scripture references, so this account stays with the settings and claims of the texts rather than adding external historical reconstruction.
ancient_near_east_context: Ancient background for Sanctification includes covenant life, temple worship, royal ideology, wisdom teaching, and early church confession; the entry ties that world to Leviticus 20:7-8, John 17:17-19, perseverance, and grace without letting comparison replace the biblical witness.
canonical_context: Leviticus grounds Israel’s call to holiness in God’s holiness. John 17 presents sanctification in relation to truth and Jesus’ mission. Romans 6 and 1 Thessalonians connect holy life to bodily conduct, while Hebrews describes holiness as something to pursue. This set presents holiness as both a gift or calling from God and a lived response.
literary_context: Leviticus gives covenant instruction; John records a prayer; Romans argues from participation in Christ’s death and life; 1 Thessalonians offers pastoral instruction; Hebrews gives an exhortation. The genres show why sanctification appears as command, petition, consequence, and pursuit across these passages.
covenantal_significance: Leviticus links Israel’s consecration to the Lord’s holiness. John 17 asks God to sanctify the disciples in truth, and the letters describe conduct fitting their relation to God. Together, the passages connect divine calling and formation with choices made in embodied life.
canonical_role: This entry gathers passages in which holiness is commanded, prayed for, and pursued. They help readers see both God’s role in setting apart and the practical conduct the texts associate with that calling.

related_objects.notes: The cluster distinguishes embodied holiness and transformation from purity shame, permanent caste, coercion, and abuse concealment.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Sanctification in its immediate context before generalizing.
Do not flatten distinct passages into one slogan; let the canon keep its own shape.
